utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. All the accused are present. Amongst the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Haynes, Mr. Bourgon, and Mr. Ostojic. All right. Prosecution, we have Mr. McCloskey. I am not seeing anyone else. There are two pending motions that I'm going to or we are going to decide before we proceed with the sitting, and that's because there is no opposition from the Prosecution and we'll avoid you the trouble of having to read a written decision. The first one relates to an urgent motion by accused Vujadin Popovic filed confidentially on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was saying the first decision relates to an urgent motion by accused Popovic to amend his Rule 65 ter exhibit list with three new documents, which was filed confidentially on the 12th of June. As I said, there is no opposition on the part of the Prosecution, and, therefore, Mr. Zivanovic, this motion is hereby being granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The second motion we are deciding today is one by General Miletic filed also on the 12th of June 2008, in which Madam Fauveau for her client seeks calling two witnesses pursuant to Rule 92 ter of our rules, instead of viva voce witnesses as they were planned to be earlier on. Again, there is no opposition on the part of the Prosecution, and, therefore, the motion is also being hereby granted. Having said that, I think we throw our eyes in the direction of the place where the new witness, Mr. Rakic, will be testifying by videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My first duty, Mr. Rakic, is to wish you a good morning and make sure you can hear me, and that you are receiving interpretation in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The second thing is to wish good morning to our staff there that are assisting you. Good morning to you. All right. If there are at any time problems with the transmission outgoing and incoming, please alert us immediately. Okay. Thank you. Mr. Rakic, you've been summoned to give evidence by accused Colonel Vujadin Popovic; and, as such, you will start giving evidence soon. You'll be asked questions, first, by Popovic's counsel who will introduce himself to you. But before you start giving evidence, you are required by our rules to give a solemn declaration that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the whole truth. You have the text. I see. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I don't know about my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Rakic. My name is Zivanovic. I appear here for Vujadin Popovic; and, although we know each other, I have to do the official introduction. Could you please tell me your full name and surname?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, say something, please, so that we'll see whether the interpretation is reaching us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ljubo Rakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: How old are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me about your educational attainment?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I completed the electrical engineering school of the military academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, briefly, about your career?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: After I completed the academy 1980 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Audibility is very bad, with lots of interference.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I continued to teach in Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because we seem to have some teething trouble with the technical side. Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Some accused also have difficulties hearing the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think, ultimately, it's a question of setting the audio level on the right channel, but, yes, a technician is coming by. In the meantime, I would like the witness to answer his question again. Mr. Rakic, if you could repeat your answer, please, to the question that Mr. Zivanovic put to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rakic, I'll repeat it. For technical reasons, we couldn't hear your answer well. Could you describe your career briefly?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: After I completed the military academy, I worked as a teacher in the military technical academy in Rajlovac until 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And after 1992?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Well, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Is it okay? I just want to make sure that all the accused can hear. Mr. Popovic, I think while usually under normal circumstances, when we are in here, this leaving it here would work. In today's case, I think you will need to have it closer to your ears. Okay. We still have General Gvero and General Pandurevic. Are you all right with the audio? Okay. Yes. Sorry for this interruption. My apologies to everyone, but it happens. Mr. Zivanovic, if you could proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Rakic, tell me now about your career after 1992.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: In 1992, I was in the army of Republika Srpska until 1998, and then I was in the army of Yugoslavia until I retired in 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In which unit of the army of Republika Srpska were you from 1992 onwards?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I was in the Drina Corps, at the beginning, in the Milic Vlasenic Brigade. Later, I was in the command of the corps from November 1993 until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me in what establishment position were you in summer 1995 or more precisely in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Chief of informatics in the command of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe briefly your duties and responsibilities as chief of informatics and computers in the corps command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: For the most part, it was a small section and most of our work was to gather, process, and update information about members of Republika Srpska who had gotten killed, members of the Drina Corps in our case; as well as to analyse the requirements of command and other data, such as personnel-related data and other information that the corps command needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally participate in combat operations related to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to other things, did you serve as officer on duty in the duty centre of the command of the corps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Well, duty service, one of the regular duties according to the roster applied in the corps. That roster was made for the current month and the following month.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll show you 1D767. That's a document under tab 2. I would like you to look at the document and tell us if that's what this roster of duty service in the corps command looked like. Do you remember serving on duty, being the duty officer, on this roster?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Well, there are no modifications, no changes, no alterations, and I did probably. You can see my name here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you describe, briefly, the responsibility of the duty officer in the operations centre of the corps? What did he have to do, just very briefly, in the course of his stint, his tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: The operations duty officer is the person who coordinates the work of the corps command and subordinated units in keeping with the orders that apply on that day or have a longer period of validity. But the basic duty is coordination, receiving information from subordinate units, processing that information, and forwarding it to addressees in the corps command. That is the basic responsibility of the duty officer, to coordinate work between subordinated units and the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just some more information, if you could provide, about this tour of duty. How long are you on duty?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Twenty-four hours. But most of the work is done in the morning, and then you turn your responsibilities over to the team. You perform it with the main documents governing the work of the operations centre, the documents that have arrived for that day for the centre and for the subordinated units; and, of course, you act as the situation requires. In the course of the morning, regular reports from subordinated units come in. These reports are processed. It was customary for the officers in charge of various areas in the corps review these reports, each concerning his own field of expertise, and then they are forwarded to the operations centre of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, can we get his rank at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Rakic, I'm sorry. I forgot to ask you about your rank at the time.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There is another what seems to be error in the interpretation. I'll have to repeat a question that you have answered. When you were talking about the arrival of regular reports from units, at what time of day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Early evening, perhaps 6.00 or 7.00 p.m. - that's what I think - in any case, in the afternoon, early evening; and then later in the evening the compiled report to the Main Staff would be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have already shown you, but I will show you again, one intercept. We don't have the log of duty service from the Drina Corps from that time. We have some other documents that shed some light on the activities of the duty officer for a certain day. Could you please look and I'll show you certain documents that we have, and I will appreciate if you answer from your memory, from your best recollection. Just a minute. Now, before I do that, let me ask you something else. Do you know Vujadin Popovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what were his duties at the time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: He was chief of the security organ of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, could you tell me briefly what were the responsibilities of the chief of security of the corps? What was he supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: He was to protect the commands of units, important structures and features in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps, to prevent various terrorist groups, and that is part of his job description I gave earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have shown you earlier another intercept, an intercept of the conversation you had with him; and it was allegedly intercepted by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Couldn't be more leading than that. Please rephrase your question, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'll do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me -- in fact, I'll show you one conversation, P1201. It's in tab 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Zivanovic, Mr. McCloskey, and Registrar, if you could, first of all, identify this intercept by its exhibit number and also check its status whether it's a protected document or not; in other words, whether it's confidential or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't see a real problem, if we could go into private session for one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We have in open session. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic, you may proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please re-read the text to yourself, and then I'll have questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not to be broadcast, however. Inside the courtroom, yes; but not for broadcast purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, do you remember having had this conversation with Vujadin Popovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: It is possible that such a conversation took place. I cannot be fully certain, though. It's been 13 years since; however, it is very likely that it actually took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, the other colleagues from the corps, did they usually call you Rale?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Well, it's customary in the military to shorten one's last name or alter it in some way; so my nickname was Raka or Rale.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the conversation, it says: "I was up there." Allegedly, Vujadin Popovic is saying that. How did you understand that? "I was up there." What does it mean, "up there"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: On that day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment, please. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Unless he can be more clear about whether this is possible or likely, any questions on these intercepts are going to be speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic, what's your comments to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is not speculation. I asked the witness to say how he understand this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Provided, I think, as a question it is legitimate. However, it stands to reason that the witness must be forewarned that he can answer the question and should answer the question only if he is sure of what he's about to say. We don't want any speculation from you, Mr. Rakic. If you don't know what was meant by that statement in this intercept, then you tell us, "I don't know. I'm not in a position to answer that. I can only speculate." Then we will move to the next question. Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. This is a technical problem. In e-court, could we have the second page in B/C/S, because the document which the accused can currently see is not the conversation in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Madam. Do we have the second page now? I think so. Yes. We have the second page now. Mr. Rakic, can you follow Mr. Zivanovic's question which I am going to ask him to repeat to you, please. Mr. Zivanovic, if you could direct the witness to the part of the transcript that you're interested in and repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What was your understanding of Mr. Popovic's words when he says, "I was up there"? What was your understanding of the term "up there"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I understood it to mean that it was in the area between Zvornik and Tuzla. There was combat on that day and the elevation there was greater than in Zvornik, where this conversation took place. It had to do with the area of combat of that day, which is Baljkovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In this conversation, what was your understanding of the word "boss"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: It had to do with the commander of the unit in whose area of responsibility he was; that means the Zvornik Brigade commander, Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What about the expression, "Boss"? Was it something frequently used in military parlance?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: We frequently used that for commanders of units of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In this conversation, he mentions -- he mentions an interim report and he's asking to you confirm whether you received it. Do you know what interim report it was? Can you recall that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: It was a report sent from the Zvornik Brigade at noon. The situation concerning the Baljkovica area of combat was included, and it was probably the most active and busiest combat of the year -- of the war for that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At one point you replied, "All," or, "Everything." Can you tell us what it meant?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: That day, as the duty officer, I was monitoring all of the events that had to do with that part of the front lines, since there was combat. Part of the Zvornik Brigade was in a sandwich between the various units at the Tuzla front and those units which were coming out of Srebrenica moving towards the front lines held by the 2nd Corps, I believe. The way I understood the report was that there was a lot of fighting with many casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will read out the next sentence of his, and you can follow perhaps. You will see that between certain words, there are dots. We were told that such dots are introduced when the operator, taking down the conversation, cannot make out one or several words. It practically means that some words are missing, and we have dots instead. The sentence is the following: "Everything is as he had written," and then dots. "I was there. I saw it for myself. Some numbers were received." Dots. "Otherwise, it's not important." Dots. Tomorrow, I'll be there. Please convey to the general," dots, "I finished with the work. What was your understanding of the words: "Everything is as he wrote"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: The way it was put in the interim report. In the interim report, it read that combat was fierce and that's how I understood these words: Lots of fighting, many casualties, some data followed subsequently testified of a great number of killed soldiers in the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Popovic, in any way, was supposed to confirm the contents of the report? Why did he mention the report of the Zvornik Brigade commander to you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I think Popovic had been given orders to go to Baljkovica area to check the contents of the report and to see who from the Zvornik Brigade had sent the report. His task was to verify the data.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Further down in the conversation, just following the sentence I read out to you, it says: "Some numbers, figures, were received." Can you tell us what those figures pertained to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: You should have an order for assistance to the Zvornik Brigade on the part of the Drina Corps. It had to do with the units that were supposed to come to help the Zvornik Brigade, to hopefully reduce the number of casualties and to assist them in that part of the theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Following that, it reads: "I finished with the work." What was your understanding of what "work" that was that he had finished?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Touring the area of Baljkovica. He was sent there to verify the data received in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Next, we have your words: "You finished" or "You are done." Was that a question, a confirmation, of what he was saying? Can you recall that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me what your interpretation was of his words, "Finished everything"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: It had to do with the touring of the area of Baljkovica. That was my understanding of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That part concludes with the following words: "Tomorrow, I will be there once I'm sure that everything had been taken care of." Can you tell us what was it that was supposed to be taken care of by the next day so that he could go back to the corps command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I can only presume that he was to report personally to the corps command concerning the events in the Baljkovica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the next sentence, it reads: "Until or by the time I arrive there with some kind of transport." Do you remember what that transport was about, and especially what "from there" or "there" means?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Further down in the text, there is a sentence which reads: "Mostly, there are no significant issues, but there were terrible problems up there and what the commander had sent is largely that." How did you understand that there were great problems there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Since he was a security officer, there were no sabotage groups in that particular territory; therefore, no direct threats to the security of the Zvornik Brigade, since he was in their AOR.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We don't have the translation of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know how I can help you there. Let's proceed. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This expression, "In a nutshell, that's what the commander had sent," what would that mean?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: That the document is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Next, we have a question of yours in which you ask: "Listen, Vujadin, tell me whether anything has come in from Vidoje Blagojevic." First of all, were you on a first name or second name basis?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: First name basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What people of Vidoje Blagojevic was he talking about -- were you talking about? Can you recall off the cuff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: There should be an order of the corps commander on dispatching parts of the Drina Corps units to assist the Zvornik Brigade. One of those units was the Batajnica Brigade --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There must be a document in existence according to the reports that came to the duty office of the Zvornik Brigade; and to the data we had in the early morning hours, in the area of Baljkovica, there was fierce fighting, and the Zvornik Brigade that was under a lot of pressure in that area required assistance. There should be a document in existence regulating the arrival of part of the unit of the Bratunac Brigade to the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There is error in transcript. It is page 16, line 10. It was said Batajnica brigade. It should be Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't worry about it. It was an interpreter's mistake, acknowledged as such, and corrected. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, when you said "Here, now," what did you mean? It's also in this text. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: You're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You see further on in the text that we have been discussing, it says: "Here, now," meaning whether the men have arrived?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Whether two units of the Bratunac Brigade had arrived in the area of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you now to look in what is tab 7 in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, for Judges' benefits and for record, could you pronounce the 65 ter number as well, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to find it, Your Honour. [Interpretation] It's the list that we added. [In English] I think that it is the document from our one of three documents added today to our Rule 65 ter list, and I could ask the usher to put it on ELMO, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have the documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: He has it. The witness is provided with the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But we need to follow, too, as Judge Kwon rightly put it. The three documents are 1D1167, 1165, 1166. Those are the three documents, and they are all Drina Corps command. One is dated 15 July 1995, the other one 16 July 1995, and the other one 18 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is a document from 16 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then it should be 1D1167.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I understood you, the witness needs to refer to the document behind tab 7. So for him, that's not a problem. But we have still not 100 per cent identified the document for our purposes here. I think it's 1165, but that's a suspicion that I have. Is it 1165 or isn't it? 1167, yes, 1167. All right. It is not translated, this document, as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry for inconvenience.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've seen this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If this is 1D1167, we do have an English translation. I don't know if it's on e-court or not, but we can put it -- well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, is it also a Prosecution exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We dug it up, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can read just two sentences from this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed because we are losing more time this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have in front of you this document, and I'm going to read it. Up in the heading, we read that it's the command of the Drina Corps 16 July 1995, engagement of units to assist in combat operations in the 1st Zvornik Brigade. Are you reading this? Do you have that in front of you? It's addressed to the commands of the 1st Bratunac Brigade, 1st Milic Brigade, 1st Vlasenica brigade, and it says: "Due to the extremely complex situation in the area of defence of the 1st Zvornik Infantry Brigade, it is necessary to reinforce this brigade with personnel in order to prevent the link-up of enemy forces acting from the direction of Tuzla with the units of the enemy pulling out from Srebrenica via Kamenica towards Tuzla. "In order to assist the 1st Zvornik Brigade, I hereby order the command of the 1st Bratunac Brigade will allocate 1 00 men fit for active combat. The commander of this unit will report to the commander of the 1st Zvornik Brigade by 1700 hours on 16 July at the command post at Karakaj." Do you see any connection between this and what you just said?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I just said. This telegram was sent at 12.47, and the deadline for execution was very early, 1700 hours; that is, by that time, the unit had to be already there in Zvornik. That's how complex the situation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the following sentence, Popovic says: "It didn't arrive in time and it wasn't brought -- inserted in time." What does that mean, "It hasn't arrived in time and it wasn't inserted in time"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: It means that this personnel did not arrive by 1700 hours. That's the deadline given in the order you've just seen. It was already getting dark, and they were not inserted into combat actions. They were still being expected somewhere in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And then it says: "That's why this commander there had -- was in trouble."

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: It's Tamborovic [phoen], the commander of the Zvornik Brigade. He had trouble in combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see that you got in touch with the duty operations officer after that, precisely with regard to providing more information about these men. What I want to know is this: Did anything in this conversation concern prisoners?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, when you were on duty that day, did you know anything about prisoners in Zvornik at all?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to remove one additional unclarity with regard to this conversation. Is it possible that in that conversation you introduced yourself as Rasic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask you about some other things that happened and of which we have information that they happened in the course of your duty. As I have told you, we don't have the logbook of the duty service from the Drina Corps. We only have a few intercepted conversations from that day and a notebook of the duty officer from Zvornik, from the Zvornik Brigade. And now I'm going to ask you to clarify some things for us about all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are waiting, Mr. McCloskey, just asking for record, you wouldn't dispute that this conversation we looked at was intercepted on 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President -- sorry, Your Honour. Yes, that's correct. It's a 16 July intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to first look at the logbook of the duty operations officer from the Zvornik Brigade. Actually, it's not a logbook. It's a notebook which was not an official logbook of the duty operations officer, which concerns that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number is 377. It's a Prosecutor's exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is under tab 9 over there among your documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In e-court, this is page 144.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the document before me, and it's dated 16 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a handwritten document, is it not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have the number in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have the English page. [In English] It's 25, page 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell me whether you -- and I'm going to quote some of the notes that concerns Zlatar or the duty officer at Zlatar. Could you tell us please as much as you remember, and if you remember some of those things? On the following page -- no, no. You have the exact page but I'm referring to e-court. On the following page, there is an entry stating something about the interim report, Zlatar, signal given, it was acted upon the signal. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: "By 2030, everybody to Cer [phoen]," is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Do you remember that perhaps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the following page, 5765 are the last four digits on that page. It says: "At 11.30 from Zlatar, an unknown location before the PK Defence of our line. This was what was communicated." Do you remember whether this is you who communicated that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We don't have the English translation of the original document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the end of that page: "At 1250 ..." --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I provided the booth with the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- with this document, so if they could please make use of it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: English page 147, we are looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 147.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The ERN' last four is 5765 for the booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. All right. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In English, it is page 28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay. Let's move.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the end of this page, it says: "At 12.50, our package has already left from Zlatar, and another package should arrive by 10.30. This was communicated to the brigade IKM." My question: Do you remember that you sent this message?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. But judging by the order that you just quoted a while ago, it was realistic to expect that this should arrive in the Zvornik Brigade. Two parcels that we are talking about, they should have arrived from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you put this word "parcel" in context?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: The units that were summoned to help Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the following page, kindly look at that, it says: "Popovic requested bus with a full tank to be sent and 500 litres of D-2. Zlatar duty officer and Golic informed." Do you remember whether you recorded that conversation? Do you remember that request that fuel should be sent?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you another telephone conversation. It is 1189, the Prosecutor's Exhibit 1189, and I'm going to ask you to look under -- just a moment please. Let me just try and find the place. This is under tab number 12: At 1358, this is not the first conversation but rather the second one. At 1358, this is a conversation that was conducted between the duty officer at Zlatar and the duty officer at Palma. This is at least what it says here at 1358. I'm interested in the first five lines of that conversation where it says -- could you please read for yourself. You can read the entire thing if you wish. Please read, and then I'll have some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, judging by the first five sentences in that conversation, it arises from them that the duty officer called from Palma and said that Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic asked for 500 litres of D-2, and this should be communicated to the duty officer at Zlatar. Can you please tell me whether you remember any such conversation and any such request?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: But at the beginning, it says that the connection was transferred not to the duty officer but to somebody else in the command. So the duty officer at Zlatar never received this communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question was whether you received this message or not.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now I'm going to ask you to go back to the logbook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, if you do not identify the exact tab number for Serb B/C/S, the accused cannot follow. The Judges can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's in the interests of your clients actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I indicated the tab number to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 1189, A, B, C, or whatever. You have to indicate the exact publication broadcasting to the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. It is C, C for English translation -- or A, A. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the other thing is I understand, Judge Kwon, and, Mr. Zivanovic, that this document is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could someone check, because that's the information I have. Because if it is, then we need to go in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As long as we do not broadcast this document, it will be okay. But my point is the accused were not following this intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that the accused can follow it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unless we get the reference, the technicians, or whoever is responsible, will not upload this document on e-court in a way that the accused can then follow. This is the problem. This is why we are telling you make sure each time you're going to refer to a document. It's not enough that the witness over there has got a folder with documents behind a tab number. That's not enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I can repeat this question and give you exact letter of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That will be appreciated, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's Prosecution Document P1189, A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And there will be no broadcast of this document while we proceed with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: We need the B/C/S, though. A is the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: A is English. B/C/S is C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: C.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I could repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment, while we wait for the uploading. Yes, we have it. We have it now. Please, if you could kindly repeat your question, Mr. Zivanovic? We need to go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rakic, I'm going to repeat the last few questions about the document because not everybody in the courtroom could follow as we were talking. I'm, again, asking you to look at the conversation that took place at 1358 and to tell me, please, whether you remember that you heard that conversation. Now that you have read the record, do you remember that you received from Popovic, or somebody else, a message that Popovic was asking for 500 litres of Diesel-2 fuel?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: No. But you can see in the document that the connection was rerouted to another user. So according to the document, this was never received by the centre and by the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to the duty officer's logbook, i.e. the notebook of the duty officer that we just saw a little while ago. It says in it: "Entry 114, 1700 hours."

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says that a signal was given from Zlatar one night for the sector where the commander is. Do you remember that you communicated this message?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: No, I had never communicated this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we get an ERN for the B/C/S page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It continues like this all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's the same page as previous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could read out the last four digits of ERN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 148, English page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is the next entry after previous one with fuel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The previous one was 147.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was already shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now look at the following entry at 1430 hours, where it says: "Reported from Zlatar that 30 of them are supposed to come from Dobos [phoen] by 1600 hours, convey to the commander or they will be attached to the commander." Do you know what this refers to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: This refers to the order for the units to come and assist the Zvornik Brigade, i.e. the troops of the Drina Corps from other units that were supposed to arrive in the sector of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Zivanovic. Could you check the line 24 of previous page -- 26. You said 1700 hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. Just a moment, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it 1417?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is 14 hours 17 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we look at the last entry on that same page. It says: "They called from Zlatar that the commander," I apologise, "is to call the Zlatar duty officer or send -- that the commander should call the duty officer at Zlatar or send a written report on the situation in the field at 1525 hours." Do you remember whether you perhaps asked for something like that from the Zvornik Brigade at the time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: A report was asked because it was not known at the time what the situation was at the Baljkovica sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Non-responsive.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Interim report was asked for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's a non-responsive answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. That's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now can we move on to the following page. I'm not going to ask you about the first things where the numbers of the battalions are listed. I'm going to ask you about the entry at 1620 hours. It says: "Message from Zlatar that one officer from the command was to be sent immediately to the commander and send a written report on the current situation, the agreement, and arrangements made with the other side, immediately send Mijatovic." Do you remember whether you conveyed this message from Zlatar?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Look at the following entry, where it says: "Message from Zlatar that Lieutenant Colonel Popovic must go to Vinko Pandurevic in the field at 1640 hours." Do you remember if it was you who conveyed the message that Popovic should go to Pandurevic on that day? Do you remember having conveyed this particular message that we are talking about at the moment?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: No, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the last paragraph of this page, it says: "30 soldiers came from Vlasenica at 1705 and were sent immediately to the IKM in Kitovnice as ordered. Zlatar was immediately informed and asked again whether the report had come from the commander." Do you remember whether you conveyed this message?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This part about whether he was informed, yes, because the report came from the duty officer at Palma, informing us that soldiers had arrived from Dobos [phoen], which means from the Vlasenica Brigade units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the following page, in the penultimate paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I apologise. Just bear with me while I'm looking at the entry at 18 00 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Penultimate paragraph on the following page, it says: "They asked from Zlatar if Vazic had received any assistance. It was checked, and a response came that they haven't arrived yet but they are expected around 1800 hours." Do you remember who Vasic was?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: He was the chief of the security centre in Zvornik; actually, it's the Zvornik MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the activities of the MUP on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: On that day, Zvornik was threatened, and that's all. The available forces were engaged, including the MUP units, to assist the units between Snagovo and Baljkovica, on that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, if on that day, some reinforcement was sent to them as well? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I only know that later we were informed that a MUP unit had arrived from Doboj, I believe, and that they had problems as soon as they entered combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now let's move on to the following page, the last paragraph on that page, where it says: "Message from Zlatar that a parcel set off from Badem. Half an hour ago, it was reported at 2015, reported at IKM." Can you explain the nature of that particular parcel? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Again, this was executing the order about a hundred fighters from the Bratunac Brigade to be sent to the Zvornik Brigade. This is the same parcel we already mentioned that was late in arriving.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now explain one thing? At that time, in the evening hours of that day, there was no more fighting, the line had already been opened. Do you remember, if you remember, why these soldiers, the reinforcement, had been dispatched at the moment to assist the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: The order was sent earlier, around 1300 hours; and the intention was to open the corridor and stop the possible breakthrough of the enemy towards Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm now going to ask you to look at the following entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The page number is 5770, the following page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, I think it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have the break now, 25 minutes, and then we'll see. How much longer?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe 15 to 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rakic, can you hear us? Are you receiving interpretation of what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let's continue, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you recall -- I'll ask you just one more thing concerning this, these books or notebooks of the duty officer of the Zvornik Brigade. Well, it's the same page where you were. In EDS, it's 33rd page of English, and 152nd page of B/C/S. [In English] Sorry. [Interpretation] In e-court, I meant, not EDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we get an ERN?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is 5770.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's this entry at 2125, where information is asked from Zlatar whether "self-propelled guns are still in our hands." Do you remember passing on this information?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: No, I did not pass it on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll ask you about just one more intercept. It's P1205. It's the last tab in your file, bearing number 15. This intercept is from the 17th of July 1995, in the morning at 5.27. Could you please read this first conversation, it's very short, and then I'll ask my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's A and C in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, this document is also under seal, I'm being informed, so that there will not be any broadcast while we process it. Thank you. Go ahead, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You have seen a reference to your surname in one place here. So I want to know whether you recall you had this conversation on that day in the morning.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: That was after wake-up. When the duty officer calls, the commander calls subordinated units to see if anything extraordinary happened during the night. That is from the last regular report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rakic, I'm no longer going to show you these documents. I just wanted to ask you about your knowledge in general, since you were in the command of the Drina Corps at the time. Tell me first, do you recall whether, in the combat activities around Srebrenica, the whole corps was engaged or only some of the units?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Part of the units were involved in direct combat. Other units were engaged in other segments of the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall if there existed in Srebrenica certain Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you recall, approximately, their strength?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: According to some information, they had 5.000 to 6.000 fighting men.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember what happened with these forces after the VRS entered Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: One part of them moved to join up with the units in the area towards Tuzla, Baljkovica, where there were later some combat operations. That was the part that pulled out from Srebrenica towards Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm going to object to any more questions about this. We received information that this witness would talk about one intercept, the intercept about Popovic coming to the front lines. That's all the information we've received, and we have received no proofing note. So he's gone into many other intercepts and things that we at least saw on his list of exhibits, so we at least saw that coming. This area is completely new; and, frankly, I would object unless I can get more information, and that goes for future witnesses as well, if this is going to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: These are general information about the units of 28th Division, about Muslim units, and the events which took place after entering of VRS in Srebrenica; and the witness was the officer of the command of Drina Corps and I just asked him about such questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But do you necessarily have to rely or refer to an intercept that has -- you haven't given prior notice of to the Prosecution to ask the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I finished with intercepts. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. You could have asked a general question without referring to the intercept for which the Prosecution had not been prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll not refer to any interception, any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I finished with confronting the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's continue. But point taken, and that applies across the board to all Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'll reduce my questions, my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But it is not a question of --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, it's not a question of reducing or augmenting the number of your questions. The point made by Mr. McCloskey is you've been referring the witness to intercepts which were not indicated by you when you provided the Prosecution with prior, advance notice of what this witness will be testifying upon. That is precisely what should be avoided. The Prosecution should not be taken by surprise and have to face questions on intercepts that were not on the list that were not indicated as being intercepts on which the witness will be asked questions. This is the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: All these intercepts are on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But they were not indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's true that I did not indicate in my witness summary about it. That's true. I found it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. They are on the list that has been provided now. Let's continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware -- no, no. I'm not going to ask you that. Just tell me, please, how and when did you first learn of this conversation that I have shown you, the conversation between you and Popovic, and in what context. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I believe it was just prior to the Krstic trial, when I first found about it; and I found it on the internet later, this intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever had occasion or has anyone ever asked you about the contents of that conversation, apart from Defence teams?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Nikolic, you had indicated that you don't have questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. We have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lazarevic, you had requested about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's what we requested. But after reconsidering and hearing his evidence here, we decided not to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Madam Faveau or Mr. Petrusic. Yes, Mr. Petrusic, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. The Defence of General Miletic will have questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I said go ahead, because I anticipated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Rakic, good morning. My name is Nenad Petrusic; and on behalf of the Defence team of General Miletic, I will be asking you some questions. You said that in the course of 1995, you performed certain duties in the informatics section of the Drina Corps. Can you tell us whether this section was part of the staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Who was your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff was -- until July, it was Krstic, and later it was General Andric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In that hierarchy, did Colonel Lazic had any superior relationship towards you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Only if he was standing in for the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You said, furthermore, that in performing your duties in the informatics section, for the most part, you entered data about persons missing or killed and such; and I would like to know whether in the course of making these statistics and putting them in the computer, you also introduced information about the passage of humanitarian aid through the area of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, another section was doing that. If we were making any reports about that, that would be compiled reports for a certain period, like monthly reports, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So do you know about the existence of those monthly or annual reports? Were they made?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Some sort of overview was made. Whether it was monthly or bi-monthly or covered a longer period, I can't remember. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you participate in any way in issuing combat documents?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: No, not directly in adopting combat documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I call up 5D1179.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And in your bundle, Mr. Rakic, that would be under number P1179.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It must be a mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rakic, may I suggest that you look at the document P1179?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I don't have that document in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, the witness is saying that he hasn't got that document in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in e-court, this document is marked 5D1175; however, the document that Mr. Lasic -- or rather, Rakic should have is erroneously marked P1179. That is our mistake, but he has it in any case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it 5D1179 or 75?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 79.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Rakic, have you managed to find it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Is there a more practical way of doing this? If we put the -- I don't know if the witness can see or can follow documents from e-court, and I don't know whether -- no, he cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At any rate, I will quote a part of that document, and I don't think it will be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rakic, I will take you back to an issue that Mr. Zivanovic also asked you about, combat reports. Who made combat reports, both daily and interim?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: The person who directly made them was the duty operations officer and assistant commanders responsible for certain areas; somebody from the organ for logistics and the rear and the personnel man, the assistant for morale and other members of the corps, other commanding officers in the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Well, since you don't have the document 5D1179 that I wanted to show you, this is a report from the command of the Drina Corps dated 26th of February 1994, number 0/5-109; and the person signed is Milenko Zivanovic, Major-General. It says: "For the purpose of more efficient control and command and with the objective of maximizing assistance lent to subordinate commands, I hereby order, point 2, the duty operations officer of the corps command shall, before drafting the report to the superior command, formulate the proposals made by commanding officers in the corps command by organ ..." And, in brackets, we see, "intelligence personnel, logistics," et cetera, brackets closed. "... in the course of preparation; and after formulating their report shall read it to the Chief of Staff, make a brief analysis, and only then submit the report for signature." So we can note that Major-General Zivanovic requires, by this order, that either he or the Chief of Staff be the sole persons who can sign such an operations report. So, Mr. Rakic, do you agree with this statement?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether, in the absence of either or both of these from the command, that is, both the commander and the Chief of Staff, anyone else could sign that report, and who?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Well, that should have been the chief of the operations organ in the corps command, chief of operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Mr. President, if we still have a problem with the documents provided by the Defence; but if we don't, I'd like to call up 5D1011. That document should be in the bundle of Mr. Rakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Rakic, have you found this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have the documents at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How many folders do you have there? You must have one definitely from the Popovic Defence team; and, as I understand it, maybe one from the Prosecution. I would expect that; and one from the Miletic Defence team. I am beginning to suspect that maybe he is mixing the folders.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe so, Your Honour, because we did communicate to the Registry the binders for these two witnesses that are supposed to testify by videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have no doubt about that, Madam Fauveau, and I also noticed, I don't know if you did, but at one point he had one folder which he moved aside, then he had a second folder which he moved aside; and it seemed to me that the lady, Deputy Registrar, sitting next to him was going through another folder. So he must have three folders. That's at least what I could notice because I was precisely keeping a watchful eye on what was happening. But I'm not in a position from here to see. Have you identified the folder from the Miletic Defence team?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still don't have that in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How many folders do you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is it, from Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You seemed to have another one before. I saw two anyway. That's another one. Who is that from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is from the operations centre of the Zvornik Brigade, the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That green --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is yours?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's just the duty officer notebook, translated version, that's clear in case that became an issue; something that we sent along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And what does the Registrar, the lady, have in her hand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She has got another one there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This should be the folder. This is it. Now I've got the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you so much. Let's proceed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is document 5D1011. I apologise, 5D1011.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: It should be a different document. Actually, it should be the second document in the folder.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Rakic. Look at the document from the command of the Drina Corps. The last four digits are 8881. If you look at the top of the document, you will see.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: There is no marking, nothing. I don't have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm addressing the registrar over there. Madam, it seems that the Popovic documents and the Miletic documents have been combined in one folder; although, they are easily identifiable. If you could please try to sort this out, we are going to have a short break. In the meantime, as soon as you have singled out the Miletic Defence documents, please communicate that to us, so that we can restart and continue the sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I correct myself. It seems that the Miletic documents for this witness and for the next one, for Mr. Blagojevic, have been mixed together; and, therefore, one needs to know exactly which ones pertain to this witness and which ones to the next. This is the problem that we have. Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think this is the problem. First, they were given to the registrar in two different binders; and for each witness, we have a list of documents. The only mistake that occurred is for this witness, but it's just that the "5D" had been turned into "P," but the number itself was correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If the registrar could see if there is a packet from the Prosecution as well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- because we can had a big packet that we gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The one we saw earlier on, which you said that's from the Prosecution, that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Maybe the registrar there can address us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. She is probably --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The thing is solving the problem in relation to one document isn't the answer. We need to identify all the documents and have them ready. Madam Registrar over there, did you hear and did you follow Mr. McCloskey's intervention?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [via Videolink] [No sound]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is not proceeding as it should. Madam Registrar, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [via Videolink] [No sound]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I'm not hearing her. Can you repeat, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [via Videolink] [No sound]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want to make sure that all the others that Mr. Petrusic will be referring to, that is, the total amount of all the Miletic documents, are at his disposal. They are now?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [via Videolink] [No sound]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And what about the Prosecution documents?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [via Videolink] [No sound]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But are they available? All right. So let's proceed then. We don't need the break. Okay. Let's carry on, Mr. Petrusic. Sorry for that interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rakic, you have the document. But before that, please, would the command have to be provided with timely and objective information about the situation on the battlefield through its subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Please look at the document 5D1011.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that there should be a translation of this document as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: It was issued by the command of the Drina Corps on the 22nd of June 1994. It's signed by the commander, General Milenko Zivanovic. The title of this document is, "Incomplete regular combat reports, warning." In the first paragraph, the commander says as follows: "As we are following regular combat reports, the command corps is often -- the corps command is often not in a position to form a good picture of the real situation in the area of responsibility of the units. Although, the structure of the reports has been established, comments and remarks are sometimes very superficial, so that when reading the report, one cannot deduce anything about the activities and the focus of work of the brigade commands and their subordinate units. Very often, these reports are not extensive enough, encumbered by enumerations, without any evaluations and conclusions; especially, this concerns the monitoring the activities of the enemy and its intentions. And now we go on: "When it comes to making decisions at a higher level, such reports do not provide us with an opportunity to formulate our own positions and to make decisions that would be of any significance in long term." In other words, their useful value for operations and strategical considerations is next to none. My question to you is this: Did you, and I don't mean personally you, but the command, know anything about such warnings that arrived on the part of the commander?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In other words, the same measures should apply to both regular reports and interim reports.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Obviously, we are talking about cross purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What I'm saying is whatever applies to regular combat reports, their objectivity and timeliness should also have applied to interim reports.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to give you a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Would the same rules have applied to the interim reports sent to the superior command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: This order applies exclusively to regular combat reports, not to interim combat reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Irregardless of this report and independently of it, should the interim combat reports also have contained objective and timely data?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they should have contained that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And did the same principle apply to interim combat reports when it came to signing and informing the commander, the Chief of Staff, as was the case with regular combat reports?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, the same rule applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who -- actually, my layman's understanding of the term "duty officer" is that there was just one person involved. Could you tell us whether there was a team on duty, or whether there was just one person. Or maybe just one officer and his assistant?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: In principle, the -- there was just one duty officer in the operations centre and his assistant. And as for the other officers that provided logistical support, there were others, the encryptors and the other personnel, that facilitated communication with the either subordinate or superior units, i.e., the superior commands, with which communication was maintained.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In other words, we are talking about the encryptors possibly a courier who would have been engaged for urgent deliveries, a driver perhaps. In other words, there were several persons involved?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. But when you're talking about those people who were on duty, there was just one duty officer and his assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You, as a duty operations officer, were on duty for 12 or 24 hours, or up to 1200 or up to 2400 hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that would have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: After that, you would have been replace bid your assistant; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the morning, before the duty operations officers handed over duty to somebody else, would he have informed his successor by the assistant of what had happened during the night?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
