utterances.text: You would enter all the relevant information about the events that happened while you were on duty in the duty operations officer's logbook; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up 5D --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you repeat the number, please, Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5D1180.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: This is a document issued by the command of the Drina Corps on 17 March 1994. Again, it was signed by the commander, Major General Milenko Zivanovic. General Zivanovic calls this document an operative duty warning; and then in paragraph 2, it says -- actually, before, in paragraph 3, it says: "I issued several orders to regulate the operations duty, providing for it to be around the clock." Then it goes on to say that: "On the 17th of March 1994, the assistant of the duty operations officer of the Drina Corps called the units to check the situation on the front line. He could not get through to any duty officer in any of the units because the switchboard operators did not respond. The conclusion would be that they were sleeping in workplace." In addition to that: "Over the past six months, combat reports about the situation in the area of responsibility of the brigades sent to the corps command as a rule is -- are signed by the operations -- duty operations officer." Mr. Rakic, my question is not whether you personally were aware of this order; but, rather, whether you were aware of this phenomenon in command of the Drina Corps, i.e. in the process of reporting to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Not directly. But this kind of practice was discontinued, and such reports were signed by the Chief of Staff and the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: But you are not contesting the fact that there were such cases?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I can't say anything for a fact, because -- actually, the situation was well known as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can we then agree, Mr. Rakic, that the duty of the duty operations officer is one of the most serious duties and tasks in any military, including the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the course of your duty, for example, on the 16th of July 1995, as on any other day, when you were performing that particular duty, did you also perform your regular duty as the chief of informations department?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: No. But that was because the offices of both were in the same building. If something unusual cropped up, I could always deal with the problems in that department, because the command and the operations centre and the office of the informations department in the corps were in the same building. But to answer your question, the answer would be no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So the rule would be that you would exclusively perform the duties of the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you, as the duty operations officer, have the right to issue orders; and if you did have that right, what orders could you issue?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: No. I just had to coordinate other people's work and convey orders; in other words, I could not issue orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In other words, you could convey orders that came from your command, from your commander?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I would kindly now ask you to look at document 5D399.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rakic, when providing your answers to Mr. Zivanovic's questions, you said that you are an electrical engineer by profession?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I suppose, and this is just my assumption, I suppose that you are very skillful when it comes to working on different computers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The Drina Corps did have a computer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I also believe that the fact is that very few people were trained to use the computer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: This document, 5D399, is an order for defence and active combat, OPBR7/1, of the Drina Corps command, dated 8 April 1995. And on the last page of this document, it says that it was drafted by Colonel Milenko Lasic, typed by Ljubo Rakic in two copies; and there is a block signature by Major-General Milenko Lazic. Mr. Rakic, are you the one who typed out this document? Are you the Ljubo Rakic mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: This document was typed out on a computer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Was it you who typed it out because you could use the computer, or was there any other reason for that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I can answer your question precisely. I see that there is a marking here, "State Secret." Maybe that's one of the reasons why I typed it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In other words, in addition to your typing skills, i.e. the fact that you can type, nothing else is yours in this document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: This document was dictated to you by Colonel Lazic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: This document was signed by Milenko Zivanovic; i.e. there is a block signature for Milenko Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether this is that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When you look at this document, would you say that this is Milenko Zivanovic's document, Commander Milenko Zivanovic's document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I have the signed document in front of me. It says: "Commander, Major-General Milenko Zivanovic," but there is no signature as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: There is what we call a block signature. My question to you is whether this is his document or whether this is Lazic's document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: In subordination, whoever signs the document, it is his document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Rakic. Thank you. We have another document which is -- which will bring us to the very end. The document is 5D1184. Again, this document was issued by the command of the Drina Corps, dated 13 March 1994; also issued by the commander, Major-General Milenko Zivanovic. Mr. Rakic, was Milenko Zivanovic the commander of the Drina Corps from the moment of its establishment up to sometime in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: This is an order which in its paragraph 1 says: "Members of the units of Drina Corps, during the holiday of Bajram, will restrain themselves from responding to the provocations of the Muslim army; and they will stick to the level of activities which is called for by the defence in serious attacks." Number 2 says: "Convoys through our territory should pass safely to their destinations, and the convoy escorts should be informed about all the dangers from attacks or provocation that the Muslim side plans in order to accuse us." With regard to paragraph 1 of this order, did you have any information or instructions from your -- let me ask you this first: Is Bajram a religious holiday in Muslims? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Second of all, did you have any instructions from your command, not only in this case, but also in the case of other religious holidays, Muslim holidays, to refrain from any activities or opening fire?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: There were such instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: With regard to paragraph 2, do you have any information that there was no ban for convoys with humanitarian aid to pass through in order to reach the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: There was never a ban on their passing through the area of responsibility of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And, finally, if you can remember, could you please tell us who were those people -- can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Who were those people that were on duty in the corps command? What were their establishment positions; i.e., who was it who was not able to be on duty in the corps command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: If I can remember it well, the security officer was not on duty; the Chief of Staff either, because the duty officer was subordinated to him; and the corps commander. And as for the others, they all should have been on the regular rota of duty office as duty officers or their assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What about the other assistant commanders, the assistant commander for logistics, was he supposed to be a duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rakic, I don't have any more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this brings my examination to the end. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrusic. Mr. Krgovic, do you have any questions? I suppose not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Sarapa, the same for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Yes, no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. That brings us to you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can start your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Hello, sir. My name is Peter McCloskey. I'm with the Office of the Prosecutor, and I'll be asking you a few questions. My first question is: Are you aware of a document that is from March of 1995 that was sent to the Drina Corps, referred to as "Directive 7"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: The document that Mr. Petrusic has just mentioned arose from that Directive number 7, and I am aware of that on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So you had a chance to read Directive 7 as an officer with the Drina Corps at the time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You're saying you did not read Directive 7?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you type up the Drina Corps version of Directive 7, as you did directive -- the Drina Corps version that you went over with Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. But the wording of that text was dictated to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you say "dictated," how do you mean dictated? Someone told you orally or were you given the text in front of you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: An officer dictated it to me. The text was dictated to me. I believe the person who did it was Colonel Lazic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did he do it orally to you, or did he put the actual paper in front of you for you to type in?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: It was dictated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did he -- again, did he read it out to you orally, so you typed it up; or did he show you a written document of which to copy?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I don't have a very clear recollection, but I believe that it was dictated; however, I can't give you a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you had a chance to review the Drina Corps version of that that you typed in, of Directive 7, prior to testifying today? You've obviously seen 7(1); you just talked about it with Mr. Petrusic. Did you see your Drina Corps version Directive 7 that you also typed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you must recall reading the words that you typed on the Drina Corps section that state --

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I remember printing it so --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then you must remember the section in the Drina Corps part of that Drina Corps document that states: "By planned and well-thought-out combat operations, create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, before you answer the question. Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Prosecutor keeps speaking of a directive of the Drina Corps. It's an order, not a directive. That's the only thing I want to correct. And from now on, we should be talking about an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or operative number 7, as translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The same point was raised last week, I think. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I've called it the Drina Corps version of Directive 7. I think that's clear. I don't want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed anyway. We all know what kind of a document it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you remember that -- that segment?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You typed it up, right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. But it was several pages, and I -- I acted just like a person who types and makes sure that spelling is correct. I didn't go into the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about your memory a little bit. You've just said, earlier, that you recall seeing the intercept between you and Popovic for the first time around the Krstic trial many years ago; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. And that document was later posted on the internet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where were you living in November 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: In Vlasenica. I was in the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Surely, then, you remember the public indictment of Ratko Mladic for the events that occurred in Srebrenica in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I did not see the indictment. I saw it only later. I didn't see it in November 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you hear about the indictment of Ratko Mladic in November or December 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see on television a VRS soldier from the 10th Sabotage in 1996 testifying about the mass executions at Branjevo farm, implicating the 10th Sabotage Detachment?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you didn't have any knowledge of the testimony regarding Srebrenica that went out over the air waves or the indictment of General Mladic regarding Srebrenica in 1995 or 1996?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I didn't say I didn't have any knowledge. I just said that, in 1995, I did not have that information. I learned about that later, sometime later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: 1996, 1997. I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, I take it, in 1996, you were aware that The Hague had indicted Ratko Mladic for a case that you were the duty officer for at the Drina Corps, the day that all these events occurred, one of the days?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: No. That was in 1995; 1996 was later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, when you found out about the indictments and the charges, you knew that you were the duty officer the day that this all happened, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: What? What happened on that day? I was aware of combat operations of the Zvornik Brigade in the area of Baljkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Nothing else happened on that day, as far as you know, 16 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've had a chance to think about this ever since 1995 or 1996? Remember the days when IFOR was running around Republika Srpska, so was General Mladic, people were being arrested, people were being shot? I'm sure you had a chance to think about where you were on July 16th, 1995, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Again, I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You're not aware that 1200 Muslim men and boys were summarily executed on 16 July 1995 in the area around Pilica?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I was not. In 1995, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When did you first learn of that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Much later, from the newspapers mainly. At that time, we found out about things from newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you believe it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I did not. Numbers are variable. So I did not -- I was not sure about the accuracy of all these numbers that appear in newspapers and various documents shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you believe Muslim men were summarily executed by the VRS after the fall of Srebrenica in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: It's possible that something happened; but as far as the details are concerned, I cannot speak of something I'm not entirely sure about, especially the number of victims and such things. It's probably true that there were killings, but I really don't know the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You have been living in the world like the rest of us. You must have seen the Krstic trial, the Blagojevic trial, portions of this trial that are on television; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And having that in mind --

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Blagojevic, in fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And having that in mind and the evidence that was presented all throughout Republika Srpska and Serbia, do you sit here today and tell us that you know nothing about what happened on those days?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The witness didn't tell it as Mr. McCloskey interprets his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to add this in support of that objection. Whilst this witness doesn't directly impact on our client's case, in our submission, his belief as to what happened is really irrelevant. Anyone can be asked about their belief. It's speculation and doesn't help the matter at all. Whether he knows what happened on that particular day, as the last question suggested, is perfectly legitimate; but the previous question, we suggest, is inadmissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You want to proceed with your question, Mr. McCloskey, or do you want to move?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's not -- I would proceed with the questions. This is cross-examination. There is -- given his responses, I don't see one thing wrong with any of these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to support fully the objections raised by my colleagues, but I would like to add this: I don't think that this witness can comment on any of the documents or exhibits shown to him that relate to other trials, because he was not involved in these trials. We don't know what he's seen in Bosnia-Herzegovina, first point. And, second point, we don't know what he actually saw, so I don't think that he can actually say anything about the Krstic and Blagojevic trials, and he certainly cannot comment on these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't try to testify instead of the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We have discussed it; and for the time being, we ask you to proceed with answering the question that was put to you. I'm going to read it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let him ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I was going to read it out. Mr. McCloskey if you wish to put the question again, or to reformulate it. We are talking of lines 23 to 25 on page 57.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, sir, I'll reformulate it. We both know that Krstic and Blagojevic and this trial have been televised in large portions in the RS. The evidence of that trial has been televised. You were living there at the time. Knowing what you know about the evidence that was broadcast to the RS --

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I think we can go on. I think we got the clear message. Now, you told Mr. Petrusic that the duty officer was one of the most serious duties and tasks in any military. That was especially true in the VRS, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: It was one of the important positions in any army, and in the VRS included.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And like you said, it was your job to know what was going on in subordinate units, such as the Zvornik Brigade, on the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And it's also your job to report that information up to the Main Staff as well, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In fact, the duty officer, as you've stated, would be the one drafting the regular --

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Can I complete my answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You can always explain your answers, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think we should let the witness to complete his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's what we are going to do. Mr. Rakic, can you complete your answer, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that as far as the report is concerned, yes, but in coordination with the chief, or rather, the commanding officers of the corps who were in charge at the time. When the report is written for the Main Staff, it is done in coordination with the most important COs at the corps at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 16 July. General Krstic is the commander. Where is General Krstic on the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: In the area of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He's leading the combat in very hard-fought battles down in Zepa on the 16th, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: According to my information, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was the Chief of Staff on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Colonel-- or General Svetozar Andric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And he was with General Krstic during those Zepa operations on the 16th of July, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, do you remember him being around the headquarters on 16 July?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I said I didn't remember whether he was at the forward command post or the command post. I really can't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, if Krstic wasn't there, and take my word for it, if Andric wasn't there, who would be the senior officer around the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: It should have been the chief of operations and the assistant commander for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was that? Who was the chief of operations at the time on 16 July?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, describe him for us.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He was a career JNA officer, like yourself. I'm sure you can describe him for us, if you can't remember his name; though, I got to tell you, it's hard for me to imagine you can't remember the guy's name who you worked with.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Well, first, at that time, certain changes had occurred in organisation, so I don't remember who at that time was acting chief of operations. Some changes had occurred, so that with the best of will, I really cannot remember all the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we all know there are very few senior officers at the Drina Corps at that time. So why don't you tell us who you think it -- who the possibilities were?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: It could have been Mr. Ignjat Milanovic. That's one possibility. It could have been Mr. Andric, as Chief of Staff. And I don't know, because Mr. Blazojevic had already become commander of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is there some reason why you can't remember Mr. -- or Colonel Cerovic's name?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Colonel Cerovic was not chief of operations of the corps. He was assistant commander for psychological operations and propaganda, in charge of morale.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was he around on the 16th of July, around the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: It's very possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you also told Mr. Petrusic that a duty officer's job was to receive information about what happened the previous day. Did do you that when you took over duty operations officer for the 16th?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question to this witness was whether he had received information from his assistant, the next day, not from his predecessor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Yes. Go ahead. I think you can proceed to your next question in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So it must have been reported to you that on the 15th of July, Colonel Ljubisa Beara had called the Drina Corps and that he spoke with, first, General Zivanovic and then General Krstic. And he needed more troops to help deal with, the Prosecution's position is, to help murder thousands of Muslim prisoners that were still alive in the Zvornik Brigade area. It's very clear intercepts of those communications. This is information that you needed to know about as duty officer on the next day, wouldn't it have been?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: This is the first I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, duty --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Doesn't the witness need a warning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Josse. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't want to do anything that may be viewed to intimidate the witness whatsoever, but I think he certainly does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think, at this point, we better give the caution to the witness. All right? Mr. Rakic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm listening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We couldn't anticipate, of course, the line of questions and the kind of questions that the Prosecution meant to put to you. And as things are going, our attention has been drawn to the possibility that some questions may be put to you which, if answered truthfully, could expose you to some kind of criminal prosecution. You stand protected against this kind of event under our rules. Our rules provide that if, at any time, questions are put to you that if answered truthfully could expose you, to incriminate you, to expose you to possible criminal prosecution, then you can ask us, the Judges, to exempt you from answering such questions. This is a right that you have, but it is not an absolute right. We have the option of either granting your request and exempting you from answering such incriminatory questions or incriminating questions or to reject your request. If we force you to answer such questions, however, unless your answer, your reply to such questions, constitutes perjury, then I can guarantee you, because the rules guarantee you this right that you have, that whatever you may state in answering such incriminatory questions, if you're forced to answer them, then whatever you state will not be and cannot be used in any proceedings against you. Have I made this clear enough for you to understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So, therefore, now be careful. Mr. McCloskey is going to ask you more questions. If at any time you feel subjected to this condition, then you can intervene yourself. Go ahead, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you, when you were duty officer, review significant reports that come in through the various subordinate units of the corps, such as the brigades, the 5th Engineering Battalion, things like that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you hear about the regular combat report from the 5th Engineering Battalion from 14 --

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- July? Hear me out. Did you hear about the report from the 5th -- from the 14th of July, from the Drina Corps 5th Engineering Battalion, where in it was reported that: "Today, they had arrested and killed 1.000 to 1.500 Muslims," and they needed more fuel -- they needed fuel to help bury them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This quotation is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you go further than that? Can you explain why it's not correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There is no word "and."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. McCloskey, if you want to discuss this in the absence of the witness, we can ask him to remove the headphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can go to 65 ter -- we can just go to the document, Mr. President. I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does he have it in his folder or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, he does. But given the logistics, I don't know. I can give the 65 ter number. It's 2672. It's page 1 of the English which basically reads precisely as I had stated; and it's page 1 of the B/C/S under the top listing, "The enemy."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, is anybody able to show that to you? It starts off with, "the Command of the 5th Engineering Battalion," up in the left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I only have the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Check the back. There should be Serbian back there. You see the document I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's a regular combat report from the 5th Engineering Battalion?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: It says "14 July 1995." That's the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Correct. That information in paragraph 1, you must have been aware of that when you became duty officer on the 16th, right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: During the takeover of duty, you look at the orders that regulate the activities of the units on that day, and you also look at the reports for the preceding period, for the previous day. This is the obligation. Because of the activities that were taking place at the time and the coordination that ensued from that, because of the combat activities, I did not look at the documents that preceded that. So I was limiting myself to the immediate dates, the days that pertained to the 16th. This is what I looked at, our combat report to the staff of the 15th and the reports that had to do with the 15th of July, nothing before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it's break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's have a break now. How much longer do you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll be finished today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. This means that if the other witness is present over there, he won't be required to testify today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The second witness is waiting to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why. One further question, Mr. Zivanovic: Do you plan a redirect or not at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe, maybe. I cannot tell you right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic? No, Mr. Petrusic has no redirect. You're right. So let's have a break, 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, I want to take you back to your last answer briefly. You, basically, say that when you take over duty, your obligation is to look at -- well, be aware of the day you're taking over. Then you say: "The day that is pertain to the 16th, and this is what I looked at, are combat report to the staff of the 15th and the reports that had to do with the 15th of July, nothing before that." Okay. So the 15th of July is something that you would have focused on, and I'm sure you would have focused on interim combat reports from Vinko Pandurevic from the Zvornik Brigade given the situation up there, right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Are you referring to the 16th, because that's what I'm referring to, the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, you said the 15th in your previous question, that would you look at the 15th as the day before. You want me to read it back to you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Can I please see that document? It is possible that I saw it, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, my question was is that you would be focusing on documents or daily combat reports from the 15th, as you've just stated in your previous answer.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Surely, after all these years and listening to this case, you would have been able to remember being at the brigade command on the 15th when Vinko Pandurevic's interim combat report came in that evening around 7.00, 7.25 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the details of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You say you know nothing about prisoners in the Zvornik zone, yet surely, sir, you recall when Vinko Pandurevic reported large numbers of prisoners in the schools located in his area that evening?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. May we see this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This document should be etched in everybody's head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you answer the question, sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I can't. I may have seen the document, but I did not pay any attention to the details of this document. I'm not saying that the document didn't arrive. I'm not challenging that. But what I'm saying is that I did not pay much attention to the details of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But you knew that Vinko Pandurevic was facing thousands of Muslims from his rear, an equal number from his front, and his report of large numbers of Muslims to deal with, as well, certainly would have been something you would have remembered in that context, if for nothing else to assist Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: The whole communication conducted by the duty operations officer boiled down and the work concentrate on the units from Srebrenica and the possibility to link up with Zvornik from the side of Tuzla, and the whole communication that was conducted by me as the duty operations officer and the duties operations officer at the Zvornik Brigade was dealing with finding a solution to the situation with regards Zvornik, i.e., to remove the threat from Zvornik. That was the focus of the activities and communications that the duty operations officer was focusing on, on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you're focusing on the 28th Division, but you didn't know that maybe 7.000, 8.000 members of the 28th Division --

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, the part --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But you're telling us you didn't know that on 16 July, some 7.000, 8.000, maybe more, members of the 28th Division were either dead and buried or waiting to die? You didn't know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: We had information about 5.000 to 6.000 fighting men that were on the strength of the 28th Division that you have just mentioned in Srebrenica. That's the part. And the similar group was moving from the direction of Kamenica, or rather, in the direction of the part of the front line of the BiH army corps that was later encountered in Baljkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let's go to the women and children, then, if you don't know anything about the dead and dying. The women and children of Potocari, the thousands of them, what happened to them on the 12th and 13th? You were at the brigade command right there in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Your question is not very precise. The corps command in Vlasenica was the Vlasenica Brigade. So what is your concrete question? As far as that part is concerned, as far as I know, a transport was organised for the children and the women, by appropriate vehicles, and they were all sent in the direction of Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Which was right past your corps headquarters?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: The distance between the corps command and the road is relatively small, but there is no optical visibility. There is no line of vision between the corps command building in Vlasenica and the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But you knew that many, many buses were going right by the corps command carrying thousands of women and children and old men, right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Transport of women and children or civilians, in general, was organised in the direction of Kladanj. I'm repeating my previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where were the military-age men that had been with those women and children on the 12th and 13th?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: That part of the column had been formed and was moving towards the front line of the 2nd Corps which was later on where combat activities took place, according to the information that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you're not aware that well over a thousand able-bodied men were separated from their familiar lies, right there in Potocari, right on video. It's on video. It's on video that's been played in this case over the years several times. You were not aware that military-aged men were separated in Potocari; is that what you're telling this Court?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I did not say that subsequently, when I saw the video footage, I did not see that. But I'm talking about precisely at that particular date, the 16th, July, 1995. I'm talking about that. I'm not talking about what we could see in 1999, 2000, or some other subsequent years. And, second of all, in 1996 -- since 1996, I've not resided in the territory of Republika Srpska, so that a lot of that material was never available to me. I was never in a position to see them, and that's one of the things that you have to bear in mind. Since the month of April 1996, I have not resided in Republika Srpska and have not stayed there for any longer period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 16 July, then, if you want to go back there, to 65 ter 1189A. It's 1189C in the B/C/S. I want to go to page 1. This is and intercept. I believe you went over it briefly. It's from the 16th of July at 1358 hours. This is the intercept that talks about Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic requesting 500 litres of fuel. You've already told us that you didn't know anything about that. So are you saying even though you were duty officer that day, you don't know anything about this 500 litres of D-2?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: If you followed the sequence in the document, he needs somebody. C, answer: "I need the duty officer at Zlatar." So there is no question that there was a connection between him and the duty officer. In this document, you can see that the connection has been rerouted to the duty operations officer. There is no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I'll agree with you that it's not clearly involving the duty officer. Clearly, it's involving other folks. It's involving the switchboard operator clearly. It's involving a guy named Basovic clearly, and it's involving a guy named Golic. Let's start with Basovic. Did such a Basovic exist in the Drina Corps at the time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was his job?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: He was in charge of technical services with the logistics department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So he would handle fuel?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Technical services were those that were supposed to regulate the delivery of fuel from the logistics department, with the approval of a superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That was my next question. Basovic, on his own, cannot distribute 500 litres of this very valuable fuel without the approval of a superior officer. What superior officer would that have been at this time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: The assistant for logistics, I believe, was Colonel Acanovic, but you should read the document. In one part, it says that some of it has been loaded, 500 litres of oil has already been loaded. So that is probably part of that. Actually, two tonnes have been loaded, and those two tonnes are already on route to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can an assistant commander such as Acanovic -- well, remind us who Acanovic was at the time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I believe that he was the assistant for logistics in the corps. I believe that that was his role at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As assistant commander for logistics, could he approve on his own, without going to his commander, 500 litres of fuel to go out to a brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: If it was part of the planned activities, then it is possible. These two tonnes could have been part of the plan. If not, then he should have consulted the corps commander or the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, given that Popovic is calling up and asking for this fuel, we can see that this plan, that it was not incorporated is immediately part of the plan. So now let's see. We have got Basovic, logistics guy involved; we've got the assistant commander; and we've got his commander. So the assistant, that would have been Krstic or someone else that was in command at the time, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you answer that question. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to object because Popovic was not part of this conversation. He was not collocutor in this conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we can all see that this is involving Popovic, and there is other evidence that I'm referring to where Popovic is calling, asking for this fuel, and that's clearly been established. It's not my intention to bring up every single document and put it on the screen when I refer to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You can easily rephrase the question by altering the first two lines, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Looking at the Zvornik Brigade duty officer notebook, there is a notation at ERN 5766 at 1400 hours. This is 65 ter 377, and it says: "At 1400 hours, Popovic requested a bus with a full tank and 500 litres of D-2." Then it says: "Zlatar duty officer and Golic informed." So let's go over a bit who knows about this. First of all, we have got Popovic that calls, according to the Zvornik Brigade duty officer notebook; then there is -- in the intercept of 1189, there is a discussion with Basovic about it; and then it flips on to a discussion with Golic about it. And you can see on the second page of the B/C/S, a reference, it says: "Golic, Pop just called me and told me to contact you. 500 litres of D-2," et cetera, et cetera. So remind us who Golic is, the next participant in this situation.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: From this document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry. You got cut off a bit. Can you tell us who Golic was at the time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: He was an intelligence officer at the local intelligence organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was he present on 16 July in the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: According to this document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So, on the 16th, we have a situation where neither Krstic nor Andric are at the corps; they are in Zepa. And we've got a situation with fuel where Basovic knows about it; assistant commander should know about it; their commander should know about it; the intelligence officer, Golic, has been informed. Think back, sir. You remember this?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: What specifically? Can you ask me a specific question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The fuel, what was the fuel used for?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You remember the fuel now, though, don't you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: No. I only remember from the documents that I see that the fuel was requested. From this document that I'm showing you, your number 5443, I can see that from the two tonnes that were loaded up there, I suppose that is the fuel planned for the Zvornik Brigade, according to this request.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who is Colonel Trkulja?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I think, at that time, he was in the Main Staff. He's not one of the commanding officers of the Drina Corps, therefore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember him coming by the Drina Corps on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: We did not meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know what Cerovic meant when he called up the Zvornik Brigade and said: "Trkulja was here, and it's time to do triage on the prisoners," something to that effect?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: No, no. These are questions you should ask of someone else. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did you do the next day, 17 July?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I think I was at the command of the corps, on my regular duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me take you to an intercept. Perhaps this will refresh your recollection. It's 65 ter 1223A. It's 1223C in the B/C/S. First page, it's from 17 July, 1554 hours. Is someone able to show that document to you in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you have that document that starts off with: "Hello? Can I help you?" Colonel Cerovic. Then X says: "Tell me, is Colonel Rakic there?" Is that the one you're studying?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, just take a minute and read down through there. I think you can see that they are looking for you, and somebody puts you through, and X says, "Hello, Raka." You see that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You testified in direct examination that you had two nicknames, Rale and Raka. So does this -- is this you, as far as you can tell?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Possibly, possibly. I think that -- I think that's me. I think that's me. But this is the 17th. It's possible I was in Zvornik. I wouldn't go as far as to dispute it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, tell us where you -- having looked at this, obviously, at 1554 hours, you're off somewhere. You're going up there. Perhaps, if I can show you a vehicle log, you'll remember, but why don't you try to remember on your own?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: "Up there" probably means the building of the command in Zvornik, to see Cerovic or something. That's a possibility as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You think you went to Zvornik to see Cerovic on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: No. I mean that I came to Zvornik, for what reason I don't know, but maybe Cerovic asked me to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know someone named Radoslav Pantic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who is he?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: He was in the Zvornik Brigade in charge of the transport section, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, think about him on the 17th in Zvornik - and I'll show you another document while you're thinking - and see if you can remember what you were doing. Do you remember going to see Pantic on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Well, Pantic was at the building of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sure, he was, but do you remember what you were doing then on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let's take a look at one last document, 65 ter 295.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's page 117 in the B/C/S. I believe it's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- 117 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's just a -- it's a vehicle log from the Zvornik Brigade that shows you the last piece of this puzzle. It's got your name on it and Pantic's; and as you can see, it says it's going from Zvornik to Loznica over in Serbia. Can you tell us, did you go to Loznica that day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: It's possible, because my father was in hospital, had been in hospital for a long time in Loznica. He died very soon after that, unfortunately. It's possible. It's possible that I went to see my father. That's a possibility. So I'm not saying it's not possible; although, I'm not quite sure. But I think that if we went to Loznica, it was to see my sick father in hospital who died soon afterwards. So I'm not saying it's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But you can't remember, not even about your father?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO RAKIC
utterances.text: Well, he had been hospitalised for a long time. I didn't go to see him very often, so it's possible that on that day I did go to see how he was doing. That could be the reason, but I cannot tell you the precise date because it was a really long time ago. It's one of the key reasons why I'm saying this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no questions for the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So, Mr. Rakic, can you see me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your testimony ends here, unless my colleagues would like to put questions to you, which is not the case. So we haven't got any further questions for you. I wish to thank you for having accepted to give evidence; and on behalf of everyone, we wish you a safe journey to wherever you are going from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's start with the exhibits. Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We have just two exhibits to tender, and we provided the list for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. 1D767 and 1D1167.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One minute, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't need the witness any more. So as far as we are concerned, the connection, the videolink connection, can be terminated. Before we do so, I would like also to thank the staff for their assistance in the course of the hearing. All right. So that's gone. [ Mr. McCloskey, do you have any objection? I know that there is translation missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct. So we do not object, but we would like the -- we have a July 16th document that is not translated. I just -- it's beyond me how we can get this far without a document of this nature translated. It's not translated. So I will not object. We have not objected thus far, but it's continuing to be a problem. A one-page document, at least it was on the list, so we saw it coming. The additional problem is with the next person who cross-examined and provided again one-page documents that we didn't see coming that were not translated, and those were provided at least several days ago to the Registry. So I would be objecting to those documents completely coming in, but I'm getting a bit ahead of myself. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objection from the other Defence teams? None. So these two documents are admitted. But until they remain or one of them at least remains untranslated, they will be marked for identification only. Miletic Defence team, you have got four documents, Mr. Petrusic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Three of which have not yet been translated. I'm referring to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They are for identification, 5D1179, 5D1180, and 5D1184; whereas, 5D1011 has been translated and should be in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm thinking about it, Mr. President. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You haven't got much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I won't object, but I would ask you to consider revising the order relating to turning over documents. Clearly, they are on cross-examination, so they don't need to give us documents until cross starts. I understand that. However, I would ask that where they know they are going to use documents in cross, in days in advance, like they do here, and if they do not have it translated, that they at least give us the Serbian version of it as soon as they get it. That way, we can determine whether it's the kind of document we need to have translated for cross-examination. When those documents were brought up and used in cross-examination in B/C/S, we are not, as you, none of us know what this is about. We are left to the counsel to read these things. Now, these documents have not turned out to be much, so I have not made a big objection. But I think in a situation where they know what documents they are going to give out, and they can't get it translated in time, that they should at least put us on notice of what Serbian documents they have. I mean, I understand that, in cross, we all bring documents in at the last minute sometimes, and sometimes it can't be translated, but there is no reason that we are left in the dark on something like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Any further comments or objections. Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to say that Mr. McCloskey said last June, on the 6th of June, that during cross-examination, he would not object to the documents that go untranslated. The Defence of General Miletic so far has had one witness, and we have done our utmost to have these documents translated. But if they want the Defence counsel to translate the document and provide an unofficial translation, we are prepared to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So these documents will be admitted. But as regards the last three, 1179, 1182, and 1184, they will remained marked for identification pending translation thereof. Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: None, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That concludes the testimony of Mr. Rakic. Tomorrow, we will have the next witness, again once more on videolink. Please make a reassessment of the time requirements; and if you think that we'll finish before the end of the sitting with that witness, then please have the next one here available to start. Okay? Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 17th day of June, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
